paragraphs.heading: Minerals that split into plates
paragraphs.text: Micas are a group of silicate minerals with one outstanding physical trait: a single mica crystal can easily be split into plates that are fragile yet elastic. This trait is described as perfect basal cleavage. The group holds 37 minerals, all of them phyllosilicates. They are similar in structure but vary in chemical composition.

paragraphs.heading: Where mica is found
paragraphs.text: Mica is common in igneous and metamorphic rock, and now and then it shows up as small flakes in sedimentary rock. It is especially prominent in many granites, pegmatites and schists. Mica deposits tend to look flaky or platy. Some pegmatites have yielded "books", which are large individual crystals of mica, several feet across.

paragraphs.heading: Why it splits so easily
paragraphs.text: The easy splitting comes from the way mica is built. Its structure is made of parallel layers called TOT layers. Each TOT layer is a sandwich: two tetrahedral sheets (T) bonded strongly to the two faces of one octahedral sheet (O). The TOT layers themselves are only weakly bonded to each other, by cations that lie between the layers. This relatively weak ionic bonding between the layers is what gives mica its perfect basal cleavage.

paragraphs.heading: Balancing the charge
paragraphs.text: The tetrahedral sheets are made of silica tetrahedra, each one a silicon ion surrounded by four oxygen ions. These sheets carry a strong negative charge, while the octahedral sheet carries a positive charge. Combined into a TOT layer, they leave some negative charge over. The cations between the layers, typically sodium, potassium or calcium ions, neutralize it.

paragraphs.heading: A hexagon that is slightly off
paragraphs.text: All micas belong to the monoclinic crystal system, though their crystals tend to be pseudohexagonal. The reason lies in the sheets. The hexagons in the T and O sheets differ slightly in size, so joining them into a TOT layer distorts the sheets slightly. That breaks the hexagonal symmetry and lowers it to monoclinic symmetry. The original symmetry can still be made out in the pseudohexagonal character of mica crystals.

paragraphs.heading: What mica is used for
paragraphs.text: Mica goes into products such as drywall, paints and fillers, especially in parts for automobiles, in roofing and in electronics. It is also added to cosmetics and food, where it gives "shimmer" or "frost". Large mica crystals put to use are typically dug from granitic pegmatites. The largest documented single crystal of mica, of a kind called phlogopite, was found in Lacey Mine in Ontario, Canada. Its size was 10 m × 4.3 m × 4.3 m, and its weight was about 330 tonnes.

paragraphs.heading: Flake, sheet and who mines it
paragraphs.text: Scrap and flake mica comes from producers all over the world. Sheet mica is considerably scarcer than flake and scrap mica, and its most important sources are pegmatite deposits. Its price varies with grade: low-quality mica can cost under $1 per kilogram, while the highest quality can cost more than $2,000 per kilogram. In Madagascar and India there is also artisanal mining of mica, where working conditions are poor and child labour is used.
